Zenonas Tziarras is a Lecturer of Turkish and Middle Eastern Studies at the University of Cyprus. He holds a PhD in Politics and International Studies from the University of Warwick, UK where he taught World Politics. His doctoral thesis focused on Turkish foreign policy towards the Middle East under the AKP. Over the years he has collaborated with various research institutes and universities in Cyprus and abroad. Between 2015 and 2017 he worked as an Associate Lecturer in Security & Diplomacy Studies at the University of Central Lancashire, Cyprus campus, teaching modules on Geopolitics and International Security for the MA in Security & Diplomacy Studies and the LLM. Between 2017 and 2018 he completed a Post-Doctoral Fellowship in the Department of Social & Political Sciences at the University of Cyprus on Turkish foreign policy and IR Theory. He also teaches at the Cyprus Police Academy. His expertise and research interests lie in Turkish politics and foreign policy, the international politics and security of the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean. Among other publications, he authored "Turkish foreign policy: The Lausanne Syndrome in the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East" (Springer: Cham, 2022). Zenonas is the co-founder of the platform Geopolitical Cyprus (geopoliticalcyprus.org).

results.title: (PDF) Iconographic Disputes in the  Representation of Vices and Virtues: The Series of Engravings  The Seven Deadly Sins and The Seven Virtues by Pieter  Bruegel, Pieter van der Heyden, Phillip Galle, Hieronymus  Cock, and the Process of Confessionalization in the Habsburg  Netherlands (1550–1560)
results.description: 181 13 INTRODUÇÃO Entre 1556 e 1560, Pieter Bruegel (c.1525-1569), o velho, Pieter van der Heyden (c.1530-1572), Phillip Galle (1537-1612) e Hieronymus Cock (c.1518-1570) produziram e publicaram duas séries de gravuras, posteriormente intituladas Os sete pecados capitais e As sete virtudes. Essas composições fazem parte de um conjunto de representações sobre temas religiosos, morais e do cotidiano, criadas por esse grupo no contexto confessional neerlandês do século XVI. Ambas as séries foram impressas pela conhecida casa editora Aux quatre vents, sediada em Antuérpia e de propriedade de Hieronymus Cock e sua esposa, Volcxken Diercx (c.1525-1600). Através de uma análise iconográfica e textual dessas séries, esta pesquisa busca investigar as disputas subjacentes às noções de pecado e virtude no contexto dos conflitos político-religiosos que marcaram os Países Baixos nas décadas de 1550 e 1560. Nosso objetivo é refletir sobre as diferenças visuais e textuais entre essas séries, avaliando se elas indicam uma proposta de educação cívica e devocional suficientemente capaz de posicioná-las dentro de uma disputa mais ampla nas querelas confessionais quinhentistas. Um foco primordial da análise recai sobre as diferenças entre os programas iconográficos e textuais apresentados nessas gravuras. Enquanto a série dos pecados explorava os vícios da Soberba, Avareza, Preguiça, Gula, Luxúria, Inveja e Ira, utilizando monstros e fantasia num estilo reminiscente ao de Hieronymus Bosch (c.1450-1516), a série das virtudes apresentava Caridade, Esperança, Fé, Prudência, Justiça, Fortaleza e Temperança, inseridas em ações concretas de uma vida cotidiana e devota. Argumentamos que essas diferenças indicam um possível momento de inflexão nas representações iconográficas quinhentistas nos Países Baixos Habsburgo, cujas variações estavam ligadas não apenas às transições entre as culturas tardo-medieval e moderna, mas, sobretudo, ao modo como os processos confessionais geraram disputas nas práticas religiosas e nas esferas política e sagrada. Nesse ambiente de disputas, os conceitos de vícios e virtudes, e a dimensão moral e teológica inerente a esses conceitos, tornaram-se ferramentas de demarcação confessional entre protestantes e católicos, atravessando as fronteiras da Europa cristã e permeando as fragmentadas regiões dos Países Baixos, que, naquela época, estavam sob administração da monarquia Habsburga. As décadas de 1550 e 1560 foram particularmente tumultuosas naquela região, destacadas pela historiografia como um 14 momento crucial nas tensões político-religiosas. Os conflitos da metade do século XVI intensificaram as atividades inquisitoriais em toda Europa e o enrijecimento confessional da ortodoxia católica sob Carlos V e Filipe II nos Países Baixos. Essas disputas ameaçavam a existência da Cristandade como um espaço de unidade coletiva para o exercício cívico e religioso do cristianismo. 2 No contexto dessas tensões políticas e religiosas, argumentamos que essas gravuras funcionavam como exemplares retórico-visuais destinados a ensinar e disciplinar as pessoas dentro dos preceitos da moral cristã, da educação liberal e de uma vida santificada e ativa, promovendo uma possível restauração da paz e da concórdia interna. Além disso, situamos essas gravuras, assim como o ofício dos impressores envolvidos na produção dessas séries, em um ambiente de erudição e estudos humanistas. Esses estudiosos estavam particularmente preocupados com as divisões confessionais e as guerras religiosas, que ameaçavam o cumprimento de uma educação moral e cívica verdadeiramente cristã, assim como a própria integridade da Cristandade. Nesse sentido, o título Disputas iconográficas na representação dos vícios e virtudes se justifica pela compreensão de que esses impressos foram pensados e publicados com o objetivo de disputar as práticas religiosas e políticas dos cristãos, utilizando-se, para isso, de um recurso pedagógico fundamentado na moral e no tradicional oposto-complementar vício e virtude. Argumentamos que essas gravuras se inserem nos debates que permeavam o humanismo cristão nos Países Baixos, particularmente no contexto católico, que buscava uma ortodoxia mais flexível, apesar da crescente pressão dogmática de meados do século XVI. Desse modo, defendemos que essa documentação seja particularmente rica para compreendermos as disputas nas posturas confessionais cristãs quinhentista. As gravuras publicadas por Hieronymus Cock, a partir das gravações de Pieter van der Heyden e Phillip Galle, e das criações de Pieter Bruegel, foram amplamente estudadas nos últimos anos. No entanto, não encontramos trabalhos que se concentrem especificamente nas séries dos pecados e virtudes. Quando essas séries são mencionadas, o são apenas de maneira fragmentada, e as análises mais detalhadas costumam se limitar a gravuras específicas dentro dessas coleções. Além disso, em alguns casos, a interpretação dessas gravuras foi mediada por uma visão estereotipada sobre as WOLTJER, Juliaan. “Public Opinion and the Persecution of Heretics in the Netherlands, 1550–59”. In: Judith Pollman e Andrew Spicer (org.), Public Opinion and Changing Identities in the Early Modern Netherlands. Brill: Leiden e Boston, 2007. p.88. 2 15 inclinações político-religiosas desse círculo de impressores, especialmente de Bruegel, que frequentemente emerge na bibliografia como o gênio criador desses desenhos. O primeiro conjunto de estudos, produzido entre 1910 e 1920, analisou as produções gráficas desse círculo de impressores como fruto da genialidade de Bruegel e exemplares de uma arte popular e folclórica flamenga. Autores como Wilhelm Hausenstein (1910) e Max J. Friedländer (1921) concentraram-se nas paisagens e nas cenas em que Bruegel representou camponeses, situando suas composições dentro de um conjunto de obras que capturavam a natureza e a vida rural, definindo-as como expressões de uma arte popular e camponesa. 3 Essa primeira geração de pesquisas incorporava esse conjunto de composições à narrativa de uma história nacional belga e holandesa. Conforme destaca Margareth Sullivan, nesse conjunto bibliográfico, a arte de Bruegel foi compreendida como expressão do “verdadeiro caráter do povo flamengo”, negando qualquer tipo de estrangeirismo, sobretudo de uma arte renascentista italiana. 4 Nas décadas de 1920 e 1930, a noção de “arte popular” e “camponesa” foi reexaminada por gerações de estudiosos da Escola de História da Arte de Viena. Ao se afastarem da visão “popular” atribuída a Bruegel, esses acadêmicos começaram a enquadrar sua produção gráfica, especialmente suas pinturas, como resultado de um contexto artístico, intelectual e moral elevado no qual o artista estava inserido. 5 Nesse corpus bibliográfico, os estudos de Charles de Tolnay emergiram como referência fundamental para a compreensão das composições de Bruegel, desempenhando um papel crucial na formação de muitas interpretações sobre as obras gráficas do artista e de outros impressores de sua época. 6 Tolnay foi pioneiro ao investigar os referenciais que teriam influenciado o imaginário político, social, cultural, intelectual e religioso de Bruegel, destacando figuras importantes do ambiente erudito europeu, especialmente dos Países HAUSENSTEIN, Wilhelm. Between 1574 and 1583, the Borno sultanate, in present-day Nigeria, sent several embassies in direction of Istanbul, Fez and Marrakech. This intense diplomatic activity, originated by the Borno sultan Idrīs ibn ‘Alī (1564-1596), coincide with a period of struggle for the control of the Saharan oases such as Twat (Algeria) and Fezzan (Libya) between the sultans of the Ottoman empire, Murad III (1574-1595), Morocco, Aḥmad al-Manṣūr (1578-1603), and Borno. This article proposes to analyze the Borno embassies to Morocco (1580-1583) into this context in order to understand how the African powers, namely Borno and Morocco, reacted to the appearance of a new political actor, namely the Ottoman empire, in Africa.

4. Aḥmad al-Manṣūr's caliphal rhetoric played a key role in shaping regional power dynamics during this period.
5. The control of the Fezzan oases was crucial for trade routes and regional influence between Borno and Morocco.

results.description:
Pedro de Ivella Ohmuchevich Gargurich, captain and shipowner from the Republic of Ragusa at the service of Philip II. - Chapter 9 – The singular Ragusan vessel “Presveta Anuncijata” (La Anunciada) in the campaigns of 1580 to 1588.
...
English summary The present essay is part of the research project regarding Pedro de Ivella Ohmuchievich’s services under King Fillip II, here focused on the Ragusan vessel “Presveta Anuncijata” (La Anunciada). The ship belonged to the families Ohmuchievich/Olisti from Slano, located north of Ragusa, and currently used in commercial missions. However, she became involved in several Spanish war campaigns in the decade of the 1580s. Specific documents discovered in several archives provide new information about Pedro de Ivella’s activities in official Spanish services. La Anunciada was probably the first vessel belonging to young Pedro de Ivella and his nephew Stéfano Dolisti. Her employment under the Spanish flag opened for both Ragusans some prosperous business and personal privileges. She probably participated in more events and for a longer time than any other known Argosy vessel.
...
English summary The present chapter aims to give a general view of the historical situation of Ragusa and Spain, especially for the end of the second half of the XVI century, when several war enterprises took place. Both countries maintained a significant relationship in maritime matters during that epoch. In the following parts of this essay, one may learn about some circumstances which moved and attracted the Ragusan captain, merchant, and shipbuilder Pedro de Ivella Ohmuchevich Gargurich to enter the service of the Spanish king Philip II.
...
Numerous Ragusan ships and men were engaged in three Spanish war campaigns during the 1580s. During an audience with the Spanish Viceroy in Naples in August 1581, the Ragusan envoy stated that as many as 35 Ragusan navi were engaged in the Portugal campaign, which took place in 1580. Large Ragusan ships were also involved in the subsequent Azores campaigns, which took place from 1581 to 1583. Seven Arragucesas were a part of the 1583 fleet of Marquis of Santa Cruz. Their tonnage constituted one-fourth of the overall tonnage, excluding galleys and smaller vessels. In both events they served as troop and supplies carriers and did not directly participate in the actual combat. One vessel, the San Nicolò, captained by Marino Prodanelli, participated in the Azores campaigns during 1582 and 1583, as well as in the Levantine squadron of the Spanish Armada of 1588. Other Ragusan ships in the Armada of 1588 were Santa Maria della Grazia e San Giovanni Battista, Santa Annunziata and Santa Maria del Bissone. All perished during the campaign.

# La conquista de la isla Tercera (1583)
...
El año pasado escribí en la Revista General de Marina (agosto-septiembre) Recuerdo de una victoria, con motivo del cuatricentenario de la derrota infligida por la armada de D. Álvaro de Bazán a la francesa de Strozzi en 1582. Pero aquella victoria, aun siendo importante, entre otras razones porque señala indeleblemente la trayectoria oceánica de la futura estrategia naval de la Monarquía española, fue un éxito que quedó manco dado que la isla Tercera continuó en poder de los seguidores del Prior de Crato; seguía siendo un bien mostrenco al alcance de Francia e Inglaterra, con todas las adversas inferencias que su posesión por cualquiera de ellas hubieran significado para España y Portugal. En este año de 1983, el cuatricentenario de la recuperación de la isla Tercera para la corona de Portugal, merece también rememoración por cuanto es culminación del empeño fallido en 1582. Sin embargo, más que la importancia del hecho histórico en sí, con todas las beneficiosas consecuencias de orden estratégico que España y Portugal obtuvieron. me propongo en este trabajo destacar su interés desde el punto de vista de la guerra naval: en este caso en su aspecto anfibio. Porque la conquista de la isla Tercera tuvo lugar mediante una operación concebida y preparada para lanzar un ataque desde la mar contra una costa hostil partiendo de una base -Lisboa- situada a más de 800 millas de distancia del objetivo y con amenaza de intervención de armadas enemigas. Hoy la doctrina anfibia está muy depurada y el planeamiento y la ejecución de una operación de este tipo responden a una normativa que ofrece a las marinas de guerra un sin fin de posibilidades. D. Álvaro de Bazán y sus asesores carecían de esa doctrina pero en esencia hicieron lo que cuatro siglos después se hará de manera sistematizada convirtiendo su experiencia, buen entender y capacidad de decisión, en realidad práctica y fructífera.

results.description: Greeks of Attica (the region dominated by Athens, separated from the Peloponnese by the Isthmus of Corinth), as well as the Ionian Greeks of the Aegean islands and Asia Minor (now known as Anatolia). According to legend, the Dorian invasion of the Peloponnese was led by the Heraclids (Heracleidae), who were great-great-grandsons of the hero Heracles, and so not themselves regarded as Dorians. The Heraclids did not take the land route to the Peloponnese through the isthmus but crossed the narrow Gulf of Corinth by ship from Naupactus in Aetolia. After their victory, they distributed control over Sparta, Corinth, Messenia and Elis between members of their group, with Sparta being allocated to Eurysthenes and Procles, the twin sons of Aristodemus, one of the Heraclids [4]. That gave rise to two lines of Spartan kings, the Agiads (named after Agis, the son of Eurysthenes) and the Eurypontids (after Eurypon, son of Procles) of which, according to Herodotus (writing in the 5 th century BC), the Agiad line was regarded as the more senior [5]. In the 4 th century AD, Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, taking his information from Diodorus Siculus, i.e. Diodorus of Sicily (in a section of his history which has not otherwise survived, some of which was taken in turn from Apollodorus), stated in his chronicle that the Heraclids entered the Peloponnese 80 years after the fall of Troy, uprooting almost all the people there apart from the Arcadians. He went on to give the names of the subsequent Spartan kings in both the Agiad and Eurypontid lines, noting that Alcamenes was the 8 th generation descendent of Eurysthenes in one line whereas, in the other, Theopompus, the contemporary of Alcamenes, was the 5 th generation descendent of Procles. There were 322 years from the beginning of the reign of Eurysthenes to the end of that of Alcamenes, and 288 years from the accession of Procles to the end of the reign of Theopompus. Eusebius also noted that the Heraclids appointed Aletes king of Corinth, the first in a line of 11 Corinthian kings who reigned in total for 326 years. The final king, Telestes, was killed by his own family, the Bacchids, after reigning for 12 years. The Bacchids then maintained control of Corinth for the next 90 years through the appointment of an annual prytanis (magistrate) from amongst their number [6]. Concerning the rulers of Athens, Eusebius, following Castor of Rhodes (who, like Diodorus, lived during the 1 st century BC, a century later than Apollodorus), wrote in his chronicle that the Erechtheids had been kings of Athens for 450 years, the dynasty consisting of 15 kings from Cecrops I (a contemporary of Prometheus and Atlas) to Thymoetes (whose reign ended just before the invasion of the Peloponnese by the Heraclids). A timescale of 352 years was indicated from the start of the dynasty to the death of Theseus, and 77 years from the accession of the next Athenian king, Menestheus (in whose reign Troy fell to the Greeks) to the end of the reign of Thymoetes. Similarly, Argos had been ruled by 9 kings, from Inachus to Sthenelus, over a period of 382 years, towards the end of which Cecrops I became king of the Athenians. Danaus then drove Sthenelus out of Argos and founded a dynasty of 5 kings who ruled in total for 162 years. The Argives were then ruled from Mycenae for 215 years by a dynasty of kings including Atreus, Agamemnon (who captured Troy in his 18 th year) and Orestes, before Cometes lost the throne to the invading Heraclids. In Athens, after the end of the Erechtheid dynasty, Melanthus of Pylus (whose reign coincided with the Heraclid invasion), followed by his son Codrus, ruled in total for 58 years. Athens was then ruled by hereditary archons (magistrates) for 209 years, beginning with Medon, son of Codrus, and ending with Alcmaeon, son of Aeschylus. For the next 70 years, Athens was governed by a succession of seven archons, who each served 10-year terms. After that, archons held power for just one year each, the first of these being Creon. Aristotle (or possibly one of his students), in The Athenian Constitution, written during the 4 th century BC, presented a similar picture of the transition from kings to hereditary archons to fixed term archons, but gave fewer chronological details and said it was uncertain whether the first hereditary archon was Medon or his son Acastus. He also indicated that several archons served together, one having the senior role and, when the office became an annual one, the eponymous archon, i.e. the one who gave his name to the year, was the head of the group. In the chronicle of Eusebius, the author went on to give the complete list of kings (17 in total), hereditary archons (13 altogether) and the 7 archons who served 10-year terms. He gave reign-lengths for the kings and hereditary archons consistent with the overall timescale given by Castor, so were presumably taken from that source, but Eusebius commented that these figures could not be considered reliable, because other historians gave different timescales. According to the list, Thymoetes, the last of the Erechtheidae, was the great-grandson of Theseus, who was supposedly a contemporary of Heracles. Eusebius wrote that the Heraclids occupied the Peloponnese during the reign of Melanthus in Athens, and he went on to indicate that Aeschylus, last but one of the hereditary archons, was a contemporary of the Spartan kings Alcamenes and Theopompus [7]. Around this time, the Spartans began their rise to dominance in the Peloponnese by winning the first of their wars against the Messenians. According to the poet Tyrtaeus, writing around two generations after the event, this victory was achieved under the leadership of Theopompus. It enabled the Spartans to create a strictly hierarchical society with outsiders, mainly Messenians, at the base, these being the helots, i.e. slaves, whose labour enabled Spartan males to devote their entire time to achieving military excellence [8]. Alcamenes and Theopompus were the last Spartan kings mentioned in the chronicle of Eusebius, but we know from other sources that both lines of kings continued long after this time. However, they formed part of a structure of government which included five magistrates, known as ephors, who were elected for a one-year term, and could not be re-elected. The chief ephor, who was in some ways more powerful than either of the kings, gave his name to the year. Whether this system came into operation after the reigns of Alcamenes and Theopompus, or at a later time, is uncertain [9]. More generally, there can be little certainty about any Greek historical details from this period or earlier, and the same situation applies for more than another hundred years into the future. The first major Greek historian is generally considered to have been Hecataeus of Miletus, who lived in the middle of the 6 th century BC. Although little of his work has survived, we know from other sources that he expressed scepticism about the details of events described in earlier accounts, and their timescale. Nevertheless, he was not able to provide a solution to the problems. The next important historian, Herodotus, who lived half a century later, similarly expressed scepticism about events involving gods and demigods, but continued to rely on generation times (for want of anything better) to provide a timescale for historical events [10]. 1.3 Herodotus and the Persian Wars Perhaps because, although he was an Ionian Greek, Herodotus was born within the Persian Empire in Halicarnassus, on the western coast of Asia Minor, a long way from the Greek mainland, he was interested in the customs, geography and history of all of the regions in the world in which he lived. The main thread running through his nine-book work, The Histories, was the history of the Persians, from their rise to power under Cyrus the Great to their invasions of Greece under Darius I and Xerxes I, close to the time when Herodotus was born.

# Χρόνοι των ανθρώπων. Θεωρήσεις για την ιστορία. (Εκδόσεις Αλεξάνδρεια, 2002)

Petros Pizanias
...
Η ιστορία είναι ένας από τους πάμπολλους τρόπους πραγματοποίησης του παλαιότατου ονείρου των ανθρώπων να ελέγξουν το επιστητό τους, με τεχνικές, εργαλεία, γνώση και πολιτική, και όπως αλλιώς μπορούν. Η ιστορία, όταν δεν αναλώνεται στην τυπική αναπαραγωγή του ομοιώματός της, αποτελεί μια θαυμάσια μέθοδο λογικής πρόσβασης στο επιστητό των ανθρώπων. Με τυπικό ρόλο να οργανώνει το χάος του παρελθόντος με άξονα την τάξη των ιστορικών χρόνων, επιλέγει από αυτό ό,τι θεωρεί άξιο, δηλαδή σημαντικό για την κοινωνική και για την ατομική ζωή των ανθρώπων στο εκάστοτε παρόν. Το βιβλίο "Χρόνοι των ανθρώπων. Θεωρήσεις για την ιστορία" απευθύνεται κατ' αρχάς σε όσους θέλουν να σκεφτούν βασικές έννοιες προκειμένου να κατανοήσουν την ιστορία, τη δική τους και των άλλων. Πραγματεύεται τα κύρια μεθοδολογικά ερωτήματα και προτείνει καινοτομικές απαντήσεις για τους τρόπους με τους οποίους οι ίδιοι οι άνθρωποι, δημιουργώντας τη ζωή τους, διαμορφώνουν την ιστορία τους και τους χρόνους της. Εντέλει το ανά χείρας βιβλίο προτείνει μια πιθανή θεωρία χρήσιμη για την ιστορική έρευνα. Τη θεωρία αυτή αναπτύσσει περιγραφικά και συζητά διεξοδικά με τη βοήθεια πολλών ιστορικών παραδειγμάτων

Petros Th. Pizanias is Emeritus Professor of History, Department of History, Ionian University. He studied history at École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales and has worked as a Visiting Professor in several French universities. He directed the Post-Graduate Studies program, Department of History, and held the UNESCO chair for the training on teaching and researching history in the Balkans. He has published extensively in journals, such as Annales ESC, and Ta Istorika, he has organized international conferences, and has published nine books in the field of Modern and Contemporary Greek History. His most recent books include The Greek Revolutionof 1821: A European Event, Isis publications, and the proposed book published in Greek by Hestia Publications. He was also the chairman of the scientific committee of the Institute of Strategic and Development Studies – A. Papandreou, and advisor to the Minister of National Education (1997-1999). Since 2001, he has been the Principal Investigator of a historical research titled "The Hermes of Modern Greeks" a digital database with prosopographical parameters of selected social groups which played an important role in the 1821 Greek revolution. He is currently completing a book on the general history of the 1821 Greek revolution.Curriculum Vitae: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petros_PizaniasE-mail: [email protected]

Dimitris Angelatos is Emeritus Professor of Modern Greek Literature and Theory of Literature at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens. Born in Athens, belongs to that generation of philologists who succeeded in fruitfully combining traditional philological training with the most modern methodological and theoretical trends in literary studies. A graduate of the Department of Philology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (NKUA), specializing in Byzantine and Modern Greek Philology, he pursued his postgraduate studies in France at the Universities of Paris-Sorbonne, Sorbonne-Nouvelle, and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales. His doctoral dissertation at the University of Paris-Sorbonne (1987) was the first systematic study of "The Woman of Zakynthos" by Dionysios Solomos, approached through the lens of literary genre theory and Comparative Literature, highlighting the work’s profoundly poetic dimension and overturning the established view that it was prose. His academic career began in 1989 at the University of Crete, continued in 1994 at the University of Cyprus, and since 2009 he has been Professor of Modern Greek Philology and Literary Theory at NKUA. He has taught at all levels of study, supervised numerous doctoral theses and master’s dissertations, directed postgraduate programs, undertaken substantial administrative work, and played an active role in European exchange programs, contributing significantly to the internationalization of Modern Greek literary studies. His research is organized into four main directions: (a) the study of literary genres and modes, (b) the exploration of reception and reading conventions, (c) the methodology and teaching of Literature, and (d) the intermedial and inter-artistic relations of literature with the visual arts. These four categories, which run throughout his body of work, reflect the spiral expansion of his scholarly interests: from the 19th century to the fields of 20th-century Modern Greek poetry and prose ‒ in their comparative connections on an international scale ‒ and from there to theoretical and critical applications on the History and Theory of Art, particularly painting and sculpture. Overall, Dimitris Angelatos’ work rests on the combination of History, Theory, Criticism, and Comparative Literature, offering authoritative interpretative tools. From archival and editorial projects to theoretical, intermedial, and inter-artistic studies, his scholarly production stands out for its methodical approach, argumentative consistency, and creative boldness, moving effectively between philological analysis, theoretical foundations, and comparative interpretation. His presence in the field of Modern Greek, theoretical, and comparative literary studies has been crucial. He contributed to the establishment of genre theory in the Greek academic sphere, offered new readings of major poets and prose writers, illuminated the diachronic dynamics of reception and the force of reading conventions, laid foundations for a new teaching of Modern Greek Literature, and opened the way for the intermedial and inter-artistic study of literature.
